681.quote_or_event: “He who always acknowledges his allegiance to his teacher, who has religious zeal and ardour for study, who is kind in words and actions, deserves to be instructed.”
681.explanation: The sutra names loyalty to one's teacher's house, eagerness to learn and kindness in speech and action as what makes a disciple fit to be trusted with instruction.
681.tie_back: As the Kural asks for a loving nature, good standing and refined conduct in an envoy, the Jain text asks for loyalty, zeal and kind conduct in one who is to be trusted.
681._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The qualities (allegiance, kindness in word and deed) parallel the envoy's love and conduct, but the context is a monk's fitness for instruction, not diplomacy, and noble birth is absent.

682.quote_or_event: “Then the King, after giving instructions, despatched a messenger, named Suvega, skilled in polity, eloquent, courageous, to Bāhubali.”
682.explanation: When the Chakravartin Bharata sends an envoy to his brother Bahubali, Hemachandra's narrative picks a man described by exactly the qualities a messenger needs: knowledge of statecraft, eloquence and courage.
682.tie_back: The Kural's three indispensables, love for the king, knowledge of what serves him and skill with words, closely match Suvega's knowledge of polity and eloquence, chosen for his master's mission.
682.source: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra 1.5, Part 1, 'Negotiations with Bahubali' (Hemachandra, tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS 1931)
682._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. A genuine Jain envoy narrative with close qualities (knowledge, eloquence); 'courage' replaces the Kural's 'love', and Jain tradition frames Bharata's campaign against his brother critically.

683.quote_or_event: “As a trained Kambôga-steed, whom no noise frightens, exceeds all other horses in speed, so a very learned monk is superior to all others.”
683.explanation: The lecture on 'the very learned' praises the monk of deep learning as excelling all others, like a war-horse that no noise can frighten.
683.tie_back: The Kural wants the envoy to be the most learned among the learned when he faces spear-bearing kings; the Jain image likewise joins superior learning with fearlessness amid clamour.
683._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (rendered there with 'Kambôga' in italic transliteration). Shares the idea of learning that excels others and does not flinch, but it praises scriptural learning for liberation, not diplomatic skill.

684.quote_or_event: “As water put into a shell shines with a doubled brilliancy, so do the piety, fame, and knowledge of a very learned monk.”
684.explanation: The sutra says the virtues and knowledge of a learned monk shine out doubly, as water does in a conch shell.
684.tie_back: The Kural joins natural sense, an impressive presence and tested learning in its envoy; the Jain verse only partly matches, linking inner learning with an outward radiance others can see.
684._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Next-best match only: it links learning with visible lustre but says nothing of innate intelligence or of an envoy's appearance.

685.quote_or_event: “Disobedient, rough speaking, ill-behaved pupils will exasperate even a gentle teacher; but those will soon win even a hot-tempered teacher who humour him and are polite.”
685.explanation: The verse contrasts rough speech, which alienates even the gentle, with courteous, agreeable speech, which wins over even the irritable.
685.tie_back: As the Kural's envoy avoids harsh words and speaks pleasantly to win advantage for his master, the Jain text teaches that politeness, not rough speech, wins a superior's goodwill.
685._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Matches the avoidance of harsh words and winning by courtesy; the Kural's point about brevity is not covered, and the setting is pupil and teacher.

686.quote_or_event: “Suvega, clinging to his courage though disturbed in mind, got up and left the council-hall, watched by the kings whose eyes were red with anger…”
686.explanation: After delivering Bharata's demand, the envoy Suvega leaves Bahubali's court under the furious glares of the princes and bodyguards, keeping hold of his courage.
686.tie_back: The Kural's envoy 'does not flinch at angry looks'; Suvega delivers his whole message and walks out steady under eyes red with anger.
686.source: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra 1.5, Part 1, 'Negotiations with Bahubali' (Hemachandra, tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS 1931)
686._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (the source prints 'with-anger', normalised here; quotation ends mid-sentence, marked with an ellipsis). A close narrative parallel to fearlessness before an angry court; the other qualities (learning, timing) are only implied by the earlier description of Suvega.

687.quote_or_event: “At the right time a monk should sally forth, and he should return at the right time; avoiding to do anything out of time, he should do what is appropriate for each period of the day.”
687.explanation: The discipline lecture asks the monk to do each thing at its proper time and nothing out of season.
687.tie_back: The Kural's best envoy knows protocol and waits for the right time and place; the Jain rule shares the stress on fitting action to the proper moment.
687._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Partial match on timing only; it concerns a monk's daily round, not choosing the moment and place to speak to a foreign king.

688.quote_or_event: “A monk should avoid untruth, nor should he speak positively (about future things, his plans, &c.); he should avoid sinful speech, and always keep free from deceit.”
688.explanation: The sutra requires truthful, guileless speech free of deceit from the monk.
688.tie_back: Of the Kural's four qualities for the envoy who repeats his king's words (purity, support, boldness, truthfulness), the Jain verse supports the truthfulness and freedom from deceit.
688._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Covers truthfulness and integrity only; purity from greed, supporters and boldness are not addressed, so scored below 60.

689.quote_or_event: “Well done! You alone, messenger, are the first of the eloquent since you are able to utter such a speech before me.”
689.explanation: Bahubali, angered by Bharata's demand, still admits that Suvega delivered his master's message in full and with force, without softening it out of fear.
689.tie_back: The Kural asks for an envoy firm enough never to let slip a word that lowers his king; Suvega speaks for Bharata's supremacy in a hostile court, and even his opponent grants his firmness.
689.source: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra 1.5, Part 1, 'Negotiations with Bahubali' (Hemachandra, tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS 1931)
689._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. A good narrative illustration of steadfast speech for one's master under pressure; the praise is partly ironic, and the Kural's specific point about avoiding shameful words is implied rather than stated.

690.quote_or_event: “Suvega proceeded, even though knowing these signs unfavorable. Good servants of a master do not falter anywhere, like an arrow.”
690.explanation: On the road to Takshashila the envoy meets a string of evil omens yet goes on, and the narrator praises the servant who does not falter in his master's business.
690.tie_back: The Kural's true envoy delivers his king's message even if it costs him his life; Suvega presses on despite the omens and then speaks his message in a court ready to kill him.
690.source: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra 1.5, Part 1, 'Negotiations with Bahubali' (Hemachandra, tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS 1931)
690._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Strong parallel on unflinching duty in the face of danger, though in the Jain frame the war this mission leads to is a fruit of pride.
